title: Claude Artifacts and Iterative Playtesting
author: InformationTop5376
selftext:
Not sure how you guys run your manual playtests, but I’ve started using Claude artifacts to generate checks for new functionality and or bug fixes before I deploy each version to itch as a final check. I find this super helpful since I had just been giving feedback ad hoc as it comes up (which probably consumes way more tokens, I don’t have numbers to back that up to be clear). Once you fill in the playtest form with your observations, you can tell Claude to look at it all at once. And then it can synthesize and spin off subagents as needed to fix or make changes based on your feedback.

What do you guys do and how are you leveraging AI with manual playtesting in particular?

comments.author: IndiBestEngineer
comments.body: a stranger playing it for a day found stuff my own playtests never did, so i stopped trusting mine for the "is it fun" part. i use them for "did i break something" and let analytics answer the rest. on one of my browser games posthog showed the median player got about 5 lives and 12 minutes in before the first big milestone, and that told me more about pacing than my own runs did. the form idea is nice for regression though, i just wouldn't let it replace a stranger playing it

replies.author: InformationTop5376
replies.body: Oh yeah for sure. I’ve got telemetry setup to see all of that as well. Actual playtesters are gold. I might have to explore post hog . I’ve got my own custom telemetry setup with Vercel and redis, but that might be good to explore if it provides better value.

replies.author: IndiBestEngineer
replies.body: if your own setup already tells you where people quit, i wouldn't switch. for me posthog was just the fastest way to get there on a tiny browser game without building anything, and the median session number came straight out of it
